content: 1. Baird et al. (2015) conducted a study where students rated their simulation experience involving clinical scenarios. The results indicated that the training was effective in preparing students to manage medically complex patients in acute care settings. The simulation training was realistic and exceeded students' expectations, encompassing not only transfer training but also the importance of monitoring vital signs, managing equipment, and adapting to the acute care environment. 2. Gilbert et al. (2021) evaluated an educational wheelchair program. Participants were asked if the program increased their comfort in treating patients who use wheelchairs. The results showed that 59% agreed, 29% strongly agreed, 9% were neutral, and only 2% disagreed or strongly disagreed. The 2-hour interactive program significantly improved participants' confidence in managing wheelchair users. 3. Toro-Hernández et al. highlighted that basic wheelchair provision education in entry-level occupational therapy (OT) programs is insufficient to prepare students for providing wheelchair services. The study emphasized the need for more comprehensive training to address this gap. 4. Fung et al. (2020) conducted semi-structured interviews and found that over time, as educators identified gaps in content related to seating systems and wheelchairs, they added more material to address these shortcomings. Students expressed interest and validated the importance of learning about wheelchair service provision as part of their professional training. All students in the Wheelchair Skills Training Program (WSTP) group recommended integrating this training into the OT curriculum, with suggestions for multiple sessions and community practice. Of the 20 students, 80% found the training length appropriate, while 10% each found it too long or too short. 5. Kirby et al. (2015) demonstrated that the Wheelchair Skills Training Program (WSTP) is a safe and practical addition to the standard undergraduate OT curriculum. It improved caregivers' skill transfer abilities and was well-received by participants. 6. Baird et al. (2015) reported that students found their learning experience to be broader than just transfer training. It included critical aspects such as monitoring vital signs, managing equipment, and adapting to acute care environments while performing dependent transfers. The simulation training was realistic and exceeded students' expectations. 7. Kirby et al. (2020) found that the WSTP for caregivers significantly improved their manual wheelchair-handling skills. The program was effective in enhancing caregivers' abilities to manage wheelchair users safely and efficiently. 8. Fung et al. (2020) emphasized the importance of integrating wheelchair service provision education into academic rehabilitation programs worldwide. They identified facilitators and barriers to this integration and highlighted the need for a standardized approach to ensure comprehensive training. 9. Kirby et al. (2011) conducted a randomized controlled trial showing that a wheelchair workshop for medical students improved their knowledge and skills. The training was effective in enhancing students' understanding of wheelchair use and management. 10. Kirby et al. (2016) demonstrated that manual wheelchair skills training for community-dwelling veterans with spinal cord injuries significantly improved their skills and confidence. The randomized controlled trial highlighted the program's effectiveness in addressing the specific needs of this population.
